A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the radiative energy loss of a hard parton traversing a dense nuclear matter has been shown to be a very powerful tool for the tomography of the density evolution and for the study of the jet-medium interaction in the dense nuclear medium.
we have shown that the induced radiation is a powerful tomographic tool, which allows to probe the density evolution in heavy ion collisions.

we have been able to demonstrate that radiative energy loss can be used to probe the nuclear density evolution and the nuclear stopping power in heavy ion collisions, and that this can be done in an essentially model independent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that

radiative energy loss is not only a powerful probe of the medium properties but it is also a sensitive probe of the initial conditions in the collisions, which can be used to constrain the initial density profiles.
the radiative energy loss is a powerful tomographic probe of the initial state of the nuclear collision.
the radiative energy loss is not sensitive to the details of the nuclear medium, such as the equation of state, the density of the nuclear matter or even the presence of a quark-gluon plasma phase.
